window._comment: RS3 NXT. WM_CLASS survives title changes and skips the Steam launcher window.

_profile_note: Arch-Glacor, 0 mechanics enabled. A boss profile is a different shape from a skilling one: the failure modes are survival and attrition inside a fight, not inventory capacity over a bank cycle. Interval is 1.0s rather than 1.5s because health can fall faster than a skilling pack fills. CALIBRATED against a 3840x2058 window with the default RS3 layout - the boss health bar top-centre, the vitals row bottom-centre, and All Chat bottom-left. Re-run `shot <region>` after any interface move.
_regions_help: anchor + dx,dy offset from that corner + fixed w,h. Negative dx/dy measure inward from a right/bottom edge.

boss_health._note: The ARCH-GLACOR target bar and its remaining health. VERIFIED: OCR returns 'ARCH-GLACOR | 24,448' through the bar's decorative frame, so the pattern anchors on the boss name and takes the first long number after it rather than trusting the whole string.

vitals._note: The life/adrenaline/prayer/summoning row. VERIFIED: OCR returns '9,140/10,597 @100% @ 780/780 @ 60/60'. Icons decode as noise between the numbers, which is why each rule extracts its own field with an anchored pattern instead of parsing the row as a whole.

chat_tail._note: All Chat in the bossing layout, which sits higher and wider than in the skilling profiles because the ability bar occupies the bottom-centre. VERIFIED reading 27 lines cleanly at this size.

kill_timer._note: The encounter timer shown top-left of centre during an instanced fight. OCR returns '0036' for 00:36 - the colon is lost to the decorative frame, so the parser accepts digits with optional separators.

backpack._note: Backpack panel in the bossing layout. Same geometry as the skilling profiles - the panel is pinned bottom-right at a fixed size - and verified here by a hand count of 13 desert sole.

session_timer._note: Elapsed-time readout at the bottom of the Metrics panel. The same geometry as the skilling profiles - RS3 pins the panel top-left at a fixed size, so the bossing layout does not move it. VERIFIED here: read '00:24:17' through to '00:24:29' across five samples, advancing exactly +3s per 3-second interval with no misparse.

metrics_panel._note: The whole Metrics panel body: XP rows with their XP/h and ETA columns, and the Gain/Drops/GP-h row beneath. VERIFIED live at native resolution: OCR returns 'XP XP/h ETA ... 71,148 877,167 5h52m ... Gain D'. The ETA column is the game's own time-to-level estimate, which is a better source than inferring one from an XP rate the watcher would have to track itself. Use gold_row for the gold figures - reading the whole panel mixes them with the XP rows above.

gold_row._note: The Metrics panel's gold row: Gain, Drops and GP/h, left to right, after the coin icon. VERIFIED live at native resolution: OCR returns '& 177,407 0 2,040,463' and the three columns parse cleanly, with Gain climbing in 455-coin steps that match pickpocketing income exactly. dy=240, not the 320 first estimated from a downscaled screenshot - that was 80px too low and read empty. Measuring from a scaled capture is not reliable for this panel; take a native crop.

rules.name: low_health
rules._note: Requested threshold: 30% of a ~10,600 life pool, so it fires around 3,180 points. Expressible only as a gauge rule - the ocr kind matches text and cannot compare numbers, so a health rule written that way fires on every reading. confirm_readings=2 rejects a single bad frame: hitsplats and overlays draw over the digits and produce one wrong number, and waking someone for that is the false alarm that makes alerts worth ignoring - this rule already shipped 'Life 4/10,597' once at full health before the parser was fixed. maximum=10597 is THIS character's pool; OCR also reads it as 10,557 because it confuses 9 and 5 in this font, which the parser's scaled tolerance absorbs.

rules.name: low_prayer
rules._note: Early warning while protection is still up. Per the RuneScape Wiki, Protect from Magic drains 150 points per minute (2.5/sec, struct 14576) and gives 50% magic damage reduction. Independently confirmed live: measured ~150/min on this account. At that rate a 780 pool lasts 5.2 minutes, so warn_below=20 (156 points) leaves ~62 seconds to react - enough to drink a restore without being so early it nags. Paired with prayer_out, which reports the moment protection actually stops; this one says 'about to', that one says 'gone'. maximum=780 is THIS character's pool and is the anchor the parser needs. The alert body quotes the drain rate rather than a remaining-seconds estimate: a fixed '60s left' string was wrong as soon as the reading fell further, and it appeared alongside 'Prayer 0/780 (0%) - about 60s left', which is nonsense. prime_on_start=true: a prayer already empty when the watcher starts is a state the player has been living with, not news. Every restart otherwise re-announced it - five identical pairs of alerts across five short runs, reported as noise. The rule arms once prayer is seen above the threshold, so a genuine drain still alerts. Deliberately NOT set on low_health: starting the watcher while already at 5% health is exactly when an alert is most needed, and suppressing that could be fatal.

rules.name: prayer_out
rules.alert_body: Prayer empty. Protect from Magic has stopped - full magic damage incoming.
rules._note: Fires when prayer actually empties, which is the event that matters AFK: RS3 prints no chat line when a protection prayer deactivates, so the orb is the only evidence. Confirmed live - prayer sat at 0/780 while health fell to 30%, taking unmitigated magic damage with nothing on screen saying so. warn_at=3 is an absolute point count, not a percentage - 3 points or fewer rather than exactly zero: the orb can read 1-2 points for a tick while draining, and the distinction does not matter once protection has lapsed. Deliberately separate from low_prayer so the two have different sounds and different urgencies - 'about to run out' and 'already gone' need different reactions. cooldown=60 stops a continuous zero from repeating every minute. prime_on_start=true: a prayer already empty when the watcher starts is a state the player has been living with, not news. Every restart otherwise re-announced it - five identical pairs of alerts across five short runs, reported as noise. The rule arms once prayer is seen above the threshold, so a genuine drain still alerts. Deliberately NOT set on low_health: starting the watcher while already at 5% health is exactly when an alert is most needed, and suppressing that could be fatal.

rules.name: adrenaline_full
rules.alert_body: Adrenaline {percent}% - a threshold ability is ready.
rules._note: Adrenaline is the one vitals field with no maximum to anchor against - it prints as '100%', not '100/100' - so parse_gauge cannot read it and parse_percent uses the percent sign instead. VERIFIED against real OCR of this row: '@100%', '@85%', '@92%' and a bare '55%' all extract correctly, while a frame whose digits are mangled to 'y@x%' yields nothing rather than a wrong number. Readings above 100 are rejected outright, since adrenaline cannot exceed it and a larger value means the digits ran together with the life total beside them. A separate rule kind from gauge because the two differ in direction as well as parser: a gauge warns on the way down, this fires on the way up. urgency=normal, not critical - full adrenaline is a cue to act, not a danger. Re-arms only after adrenaline falls below the threshold, so sitting at 100% produces one alert rather than one per second. prime_on_start=true: a prayer already empty when the watcher starts is a state the player has been living with, not news. Every restart otherwise re-announced it - five identical pairs of alerts across five short runs, reported as noise. The rule arms once prayer is seen above the threshold, so a genuine drain still alerts. Deliberately NOT set on low_health: starting the watcher while already at 5% health is exactly when an alert is most needed, and suppressing that could be fatal.

rules.name: food_left
rules.alert_body: {n} {noun} left. Bank or leave before the next big hit.
rules.out_alert_body: No desert sole left. Nothing to eat at Arch-Glacor.
rules._note: Counts desert sole by icon colour rather than reading stack digits, for the reason the urn rule documents: digits are small, anti-aliased and drawn over the icon, and OCR of an unchanging stack was measured flickering between 6, 13 and 1. MEASURED on this pack: desert sole scores +64 to +66 red-minus-blue on the icon's bright pixels (+87 at the stricter luminance floor the counter actually uses), against -48 to +54 for every other item carried - potions, runes, scrolls. min_red=70 sits in that gap, and the count held at exactly 13 across thresholds from 60 to 80. min_cover=0.2 is required: a desert sole fills only 0.22 of its cell where a bulky urn fills 0.4, so the 0.30 default rejected all thirteen and counted one. confirm_seconds=6 rejects the overlay case, where a bank or loot window covering the backpack briefly reads as zero food.

rules.name: rare_drop
rules._note: A rare drop announces itself as a broadcast, which is a different message from the routine reward-chest line and is missed entirely by loot_received. Wiki-verified templates: 'News: [Player] has received [item] drop!', 'News: [Player] completed a Treasure Trail and received [item]!', and 'News: [Player] has received [Name], the [Skill] pet drop at [number] XP!'. Directly relevant here: the wiki lists Ragefire, Steadfast and Glaiven boots - the Glacor boots - under drops announced to friends, so an Arch-Glacor boot drop produces exactly this line. The pattern deliberately does NOT anchor on the player name. Broadcasts also fire for other players, and seeing someone else's rare drop is harmless noise, whereas anchoring on an OCR'd name risks missing the player's own - and this is the one alert where a miss costs something real. It must not match the ordinary 'You receive: 12 x Glacor remnants' chest line, which is asserted in the tests. urgency=critical and a long timeout because a rare drop is the single most important thing that can happen in a session. UNVERIFIED against this account's live chat - the wording comes from the wiki, not from an observed drop. Confirm on the first broadcast.

rules.name: glacor_remnants
rules._note: Reports the quantity, which is the point of the rule - the generic drop alert only says that something dropped. The announcement WRAPS across two rendered lines, with the count at the end of the first and the item name on the second: 'You receive: 12 x' / 'slacor remnants.' Rules evaluate line by line, so neither half alone carries both facts; join_wrapped_lines rejoins them using the leading chat timestamp, which every real line has and no continuation does. item_pattern allows [g65s] for the leading G because OCR read it as 'slacor' in a real capture, and \w*ants? covers 'remnants' being mangled mid-word. Quantities get the same treatment: '1|' is read as 11, and a count OCR lost entirely ('&') reports as unreadable rather than guessing - a drop with the wrong number is worse than one without it. A running session total accompanies each alert. VERIFIED against three real captured drops: it matches the remnants line and correctly ignores the adamant salvage and rune spirit drops beside it.

rules.name: loot_received
rules.pattern: \w*b\w*m\s+shines over|shines over\W*one of your items|you receive[:;]|received a drop|dropped to the ground
rules._note: Announces a drop, whether it lands on the ground or in the reward chest. CORRECTION: this rule was originally documented as a reward-chest rule, which was wrong. Per the wiki, a loot beam highlights a valuable drop ON THE GROUND and lists the item in the chatbox, so this line is the ground-drop announcement - the two were conflated. The pattern is deliberately tolerant. Across five logged captures of the same line, OCR mangled a different word each time: 'A aolden beam', 'A golden bieam', 'A golder BEam', 'over.one', 'You receive;'. Only 'shines over' survived all five, so the first alternative matches any b..m-shaped word before it and the 'You receive' half stands alone as a fallback - either fragment identifies the line. 'shines over' alone was tried and rejected: it also matches ordinary prose such as 'The sun shines over Menaphos', which is asserted in the tests. Note the beam only fires above a value threshold (50k minimum per the wiki), so ordinary low-value ground drops produce no chat line at all and cannot be detected this way.

rules.name: gold_milestone
rules._note: Reads the Metrics panel's own session Gain rather than summing chat lines. That matters: the pickpocketing counter accumulates its own total and therefore only counts while the watcher runs, which left it reading 513k against a real 2.3M. Here the game owns the number, so a restart mid-session resumes at the true figure. column=0 selects Gain from the three figures in the row; Drops and GP/h are columns 1 and 2. step=1000000 fires once per million. The parser handles RS3's abbreviations - '1.2M' is 1,200,000, and dropping the suffix would understate the total by six orders of magnitude and the milestone would never fire. A reading below the last one is rejected as a misread since the panel only counts up; a large fall is treated as a session reset and rewinds the milestone counter. UNVERIFIED against live values - confirm with `shot gold_row` once gold has actually accumulated.

rules.name: boss_defeated
rules._note: VERIFIED from live chat: 'You have killed 626 Arch-Glacor in normal mode.' The original pattern was a guess - 'kill count is|completed ... in |defeated' - and matched none of the real lines, so this rule would never have fired. Confirmed against four consecutive kills. The digit group puts the running total in the alert, which is the per-session statistic worth having. cooldown=0, deliberately. Every kill should be reported, and a 20s cooldown dropped one of three kills spaced 15s apart in a fast streak. Nothing is lost by removing it: each chat line is counted once via the same dedup key the other OCR rules use, verified by holding one kill line on screen for five consecutive polls and seeing a single alert. Observed kill pace on this account is ~85s apart, so the cooldown was not protecting against anything real. Per the wiki, rewards accumulate across a killstreak and part is LOST on death, which is why player_died matters here beyond the immediate risk.

rules.name: encounter_started
rules._note: VERIFIED from live chat: 'Welcome to your session against: Arch-Glacor.' Marks the start of an instance, which is the anchor every per-kill statistic needs. Deliberately matches the generic prefix rather than the boss name, so the same rule works for any instanced encounter.

rules.name: player_died
rules.pattern: oh dear, you are dead|you have died|you died
rules._note: UNVERIFIED for this encounter, but 'Oh dear, you are dead!' is RS3's long-standing death message and is worth having armed from the start. Critical urgency because a death inside an instance costs the run and, without a gravestone reclaim, potentially the kit.

rules.name: food_gone
rules.pattern: you (have )?(ran|run) out of|you don'?t have (enough|any)|nothing left to eat
rules._note: UNVERIFIED wording. Running out of food mid-fight is the attrition failure that ends a session, so this is armed early even though the exact lines are unconfirmed. Reuses the shape of the fishing profile's out_of_supplies rule, which was written from the same family of messages.

rules.name: session_hour
rules._note: Reads the Metrics panel's own elapsed timer rather than counting wall-clock time in the watcher. That is the better source: it is the number already on screen, it pauses when the player pauses it, and it survives a watcher restart because the game owns it. step=3600 fires once per hour, and a timer reset rewinds the milestone counter so a fresh session starts clean. The parser anchors on [0-5] for the minute and second fields, so a garbled frame such as '00:82:09' is rejected rather than becoming a bogus elapsed time. Sound is deliberately distinct from the loot and kill alerts - an hourly milestone is informational, not something to react to.

rules.name: fight_stalled
rules.alert_body: No combat evidence for {quiet:.0f}s. Disconnected, dead, or the instance ended.
rules._note: DISABLED pending live measurement. The concept is sound - silence means the fight stopped - but RS3 does not print a chat line per hit with default settings, so this rule has no reliable recurring signal to watch. Enabling it without measuring the true inter-message gap would reproduce the false-positive storm the thieving profile hit, where a stop rule fired four times in three minutes while the activity was demonstrably continuing. Measure first, then set stop_seconds from the observed p99.

rules.name: level_up
rules._note: Fires on any skill level-up, combat skills included - Attack, Strength, Defence and Constitution all produce the same 'advanced a <Skill> level' line, so no separate combat rule is needed. The last alternative additionally catches the overall combat level changing ('You are now a combat level 138'), which is a distinct and rarer event: per the wiki, combat level derives from Attack, Strength/Ranged/Magic/Necromancy, Defence and Constitution, so a single Attack level may or may not raise it. Deliberately does NOT require the leading 'Congratulations', because RS3 splits some notices across lines and the level line alone must still match - the same two-line shape that made the stun rule match the wrong line. Checked against 10 phrasings plus OCR-garbled forms, and against near misses that must stay silent: 'You need level 75 Attack to wield this', 'Total level: 1544', and 'Your combat level is high enough'. UNVERIFIED against this account's live chat - confirm the wording on the next level-up and tighten if it differs.
